10	
11	| Step | You write | The library gives you |
12	| --- | --- | --- |
13	| 1 Scaffold | nothing | `npx create-aura3d@latest my-game --template mini-game` |
14	| 2 Simulation | one pure TypeScript module | `createCountedRng`, fixed step constant |
15	| 3 Assets | a manifest of GLBs | `defineModelAssets` (same-origin URL, sha256, provenance) |

17	| 5 Loop | step and present functions | `createFixedStepLoop` |
18	| 6 QA | state snapshot | `installQaHooks`, `readQaParams` |

I'll keep it simple by calling createAuraApp directly with my own DOM HUD, running my own rAF loop for the simulation step and node updates rather than relying solely on app.onFrame, while letting the engine handle its own rendering.

For the layout, the runner stays fixed at the origin while hurdles, posts, and track markings move toward the camera along the z-axis, using pools of reusable primitive nodes whose positions I update each frame via setPosition rather than creating new instances. I still need to check the setScale signature to figure out how to vary hurdle heights at spawn time.

I'm setting up the scene with an outdoor-day preset and adding my own ground box since the preset likely won't include one. I'm placing the runner at the origin with the world scrolling toward +z, positioning the camera behind and above looking slightly downward, and laying out a dark ground plane with a lighter track strip running into the distance.

For motion, I'm computing positions for scrolling lane markings, side posts, and trees using modular arithmetic so pooled objects recycle as they pass the camera. For hurdles, I'm working out spawn distances and heights using a seeded generator, checking the jump physics (initial velocity and gravity) to make sure the runner's jump arc clears the tallest hurdles with reasonable timing.

Now I'm refining the minimum spacing between hurdles so it scales with runner speed—ensuring there's enough gap for a full jump-and-recovery cycle before the next hurdle appears, with some randomness added on top.

I'm also varying hurdle heights and defining collision detection by comparing the runner's vertical position and depth overlap against each hurdle's bounding box. For performance, I'm planning to recycle a pool of hurdle objects rather than creating new ones, repositioning them off-screen when they're out of the active range instead of toggling visibility.

Simple single-box hurdle visuals will do, colored distinctly, rather than two posts and a bar. For scoring, I'll floor the distance to an integer meters value, with a win triggering exactly at 500. Restart via R resets to the ready state at distance 0, while a jump input after the run ends also restarts.

Now I'm figuring out the runner's shape: a body box, head sphere, and two legs that swing while running, each positioned independently in world space each frame rather than nested in a group.

For the leg swing, I'm working out the rotation math so each leg pivots around its hip joint instead of its own center, computing the offset position using cosine/sine of the swing angle.

For jump input, I'm planning to listen for Space, ArrowUp, and KeyW keydowns plus pointerdown on the canvas, making sure clicks outside the canvas don't trigger it unintentionally.

For the HUD, I'll put a DOM div below the canvas in normal page flow, with a separate overlay absolutely positioned over the canvas for the game-over state, using a fixed-step physics loop with clamped delta time and substeps for stability.

Camera stays static with a perspective setup, and I'm trusting the app's built-in resizing to fit its parent container.

Since the canvas already has fixed 640x360 attributes, I'll pass resize:false so it doesn't fight with the pixelRatio settings, trusting the renderer to respect the canvas dimensions as-is rather than forcing the body layout to auto-adjust around it.

Fog from the preset will help mask distant object pop-in; I'm planning the ground as a large box geometry, the track as a separate narrower gray box above it, with static side stripes for edges. Now I'm working through how to report simulation state each frame — particularly what "speed" should read when the car is idle in ready state.

I'm settling on reporting a base speed value when ready, the current live speed while playing, and zero once the run ends (win or lose), accepting some risk if a test expects speed to persist after loss. For the seed, I'll support a `?seed=` query param defaulting to a fixed value, with restarts reusing the same seed so runs are reproducible, and scenery stays static while in ready state until the run phase drives the animation.

Now I'm setting up the scene node pool: giving each pooled node a unique runtime id via a small helper, lazily fetching and caching node handles after the app is ready, building trees as trunk-plus-canopy groups spaced along both sides, and tallying up the total node counts across posts, dashes, trees, hurdles, and the runner rig.

Next I'm working out the scroll math for cycling objects infinitely: computing each node's z-position as a wrapped modulo of its spacing and total traveled distance, so objects loop from the far end back to near the camera once they pass out of view, with a near cutoff defined relative to the camera and runner positions.

For hurdles, I'm planning a pooled-slot system: track which hurdles are currently active based on their distance relative to the runner, reuse slots by hurdle id, hide unused slots offscreen, and keep generating new hurdles ahead so the track never runs dry, starting no earlier than 25 meters in. Then I'm defining the collision check comparing the runner's position against nearby hurdles within a small tolerance.

Now I'm sketching the runner's body: hips, legs, torso, head, and arms as grouped shapes positioned relative to jump height, with a simple color scheme (orange shirt, blue pants, skin tone), and starting to think through a sine-based leg swing animation tied to running speed.

For the HUD, I'm planning spans for distance, best score, and status, plus an overlay that's hidden during normal play but shows a win/lose message with restart instructions, and a separate ready-to-start hint. Best distance tracks across runs in the session, and I'm setting up TASK_READY to flip true after the first frame renders, exposing needed globals on window.

I'm double-checking edge cases: the win condition triggers at distance 500 while hurdle collisions are properly skipped, and if app.ready() rejects nothing runs, which seems acceptable.

I'm also verifying hurdle physics—jump height, airtime, and minimum spacing based on speed all check out, so the logic should hold.

input.summary:
I wrote the endless runner in `src/main.ts`. It typechecks, but I haven't run it in a browser or run `vite build`, so the visuals, controls and `window.__TASK_STATE__` values are untested.

- **Gameplay:** The runner stays still while the track dashes, side posts, trees and hurdles scroll toward the camera. Speed rises from 8 m/s to 20 m/s over 500 m. Jumping works from Space, ArrowUp, W or a click/tap. It has a gravity arc and no double jump. Hurdles have random heights and gaps from a seeded generator (default seed 12345, or `?seed=N`), so a given seed repeats. Hitting a hurdle sets `lost`, and reaching 500 m sets `won`.
- **Restart:** R, or a jump input after the run ends, resets the run to distance 0 with status `ready`. That also reseeds the generator, so every restart plays the same hurdle layout. I chose `ready` over starting play immediately because the task left it open.
- **HUD:** A DOM bar under the canvas shows distance, session best and status. An overlay appears over the canvas when the run is `ready` (start hint) and on `won`/`lost` (restart hint).
- **State and rendering:** `window.__TASK_STATE__` is updated every frame. The `speed` field is 0 whenever the run isn't `playing`, including after `won` or `lost`. `window.__TASK_READY__` is set after the first frame. A `requestAnimationFrame` loop runs the game logic, and Aura3D's own loop does the drawing. The canvas isn't resized because I passed `resize: false` to `createAuraApp`.
